solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Section husband over wife’s performance (4)

indicatorNotes.over: in an across clue, 'over' puts husband before what follows it

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for section
H = husband, as in marriage registers
O = over, the cricket scoring abbreviation
W = wife

annotation.surface: A reviewer judging one part of a couple's joint stage act.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Over' does double duty only in the surface; in the wordplay it is simply O, the scorebook abbreviation for an over in cricket.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: any staged performance, from a West End play to a TV programme, can be called one.

entries.clue: Laugh about covering American and European cost of transportation (7)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' means turned around, so the letters of LAUGH get rearranged
indicatorNotes.covering: the rearranged LAUGH goes round, or covers, the A

blocks.note: LAUGH rearranged, then opened up to hold A
A = American, placed inside HAUL…G
E = European, added on the end

annotation.surface: A comedian mocking the bill for shipping goods across the Atlantic.
annotation.walkthrough: The trick is that 'Laugh' is not HA here: its own five letters are rearranged into HAUL…G, which wraps around A before E is tacked on.
annotation.definitionFit: Haulage is the charge made for carrying goods by road or rail.

entries.clue: Keep an eye out for one with hands around your wrist (5)

annotation.definition2: one with hands around your wrist

blocks.note: a verb: to look out for, stay alert to

blocks.clueFragment: one with hands around your wrist
blocks.note: a wristwatch has hands and sits round the wrist

annotation.surface: A warning to look out for someone grabbing you by the wrist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One with hands around your wrist' sounds like an assailant, but the hands are a clock's and the thing itself sits around the wrist.
annotation.definitionFit: To watch for something is to keep an eye out for it; a watch is the timepiece worn on the wrist.

entries.clue: Come after job daughter had (8)

blocks.note: a post is a job
D = daughter, as in family trees
to have a meal is to eat it, so 'had' = ATE

annotation.surface: Someone taking over a job that their daughter once held.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Had' in the sense of 'had dinner' gives ATE, not a form of 'have'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of time: an event that follows another is later in date than it.

entries.clue: Foreign character’s backed internet service provider (3)

indicatorNotes.backed: 'backed' means sent backwards, so ISP is read in reverse

blocks.note: ISP is the usual abbreviation for an internet service provider

annotation.surface: A foreign-owned broadband company attracting outside investment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Foreign character' is crossword shorthand for a Greek letter; PSI is the 23rd.
annotation.definitionFit: Psi is a letter of the Greek alphabet, so a foreign character.

entries.clue: Characteristic of mounted US soldier’s personality (9)

indicatorNotes.mounted: in a down clue, 'mounted' sends GI'S upwards, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: a GI is an American soldier; GI'S read backwards gives SIG
one's nature is one's personality

annotation.surface: A trait of a US cavalryman's character.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mounted' paints a soldier on horseback, but in a down clue it means the letters climb upwards, reversing GI'S.
annotation.definitionFit: A signature, used as an adjective, is characteristic: a signature dish is the one a chef is known for.
annotation.definitionNote: SIGNATURE is a noun used attributively, matching 'Characteristic' as an adjective (a signature move).

entries.clue: Trouble is I’d burst all over the place (7)

indicatorNotes.all over the place: letters that are all over the place are scattered and need rearranging

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: Someone confessing their bag or balloon split and scattered everywhere.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'I’d' is ignored, leaving the seven letters I, D, B, U, R, S, T.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'Sorry to trouble you' and 'Sorry to bother you' mean the same interruption.

entries.clue: Shorter legwear saving money? (5)

indicatorNotes.Shorter: a shorter word has been cut down, here losing its last letter

blocks.note: a close-fitting nylon garment for the legs, with its final letter cut

annotation.surface: Cutting down trousers or tights to save a bit of cash.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose definition: someone tight with money is stingy, always saving it.
annotation.definitionFit: A tight person is careful with money, forever saving it.

entries.clue: Lively coach beginning to train swimmer (8)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: the beginning of 'train' is its first letter, T

blocks.note: a coach is a kind of bus
first letter of 'train'
ling is a sea fish, so a swimmer

annotation.surface: An energetic swimming coach getting a trainee started.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coach' and 'train' look like sports talk, but coach is a vehicle; 'swimmer' is crossword shorthand for any fish, here the ling.
annotation.definitionFit: A bustling place or person is busy and lively.

entries.clue: Chat about a great story (4)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' means turned round, so GAS is read backwards

blocks.note: to gas is to chatter idly
taken as it stands

annotation.surface: Two people gossiping about a terrific tale.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gas' as idle talk is informal British usage; turned round it gives SAG, and the clue's own 'a' finishes it.
annotation.definitionFit: A saga is a long, epic story, originally a Norse tale of heroes.

entries.clue: Clean city (4)

blocks.note: a verb: to wash someone in a tub
a Roman spa city in Somerset, England

annotation.walkthrough: Bath is a Roman spa city in the west of England; in British English 'bath' is also a verb, to wash someone in a tub.
annotation.definitionFit: A British verb sense (washing a baby in a tub) plus a proper name: the Somerset city famous for its Roman spa.

entries.clue: Empty out all contents of bevy pack Mum hated (8)

indicatorNotes.all contents of: the contents of each word are its insides, everything but the first and last letters

blocks.note: inside of bEVy
inside of pACk
inside of mUm
inside of hATEd

annotation.surface: A mother who loathed her drinks crate clearing it out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'All contents' asks for the insides of every word that follows, not one hidden run; four gutted words join up.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: clearing everyone out of a building, or clearing the contents out of a vessel.

entries.clue: Join after dropping new friend forever (9)

indicatorNotes.after dropping: in a down clue, dropping the N moves it lower, so it comes after the rest of ENTER

blocks.note: ENTER, to join, with its N taken out
N = new, dropped to the bottom of ENTER
an ally is a friend

annotation.surface: Signing up to a club after losing a new pal, for good.
annotation.walkthrough: ENTER becomes ETERN because its N is literally dropped down the column, a device that only works in a down clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both adverbs mean without end, for all time.

entries.clue: Scottish legend to take part in Innes siege (6)

indicatorNotes.take part in: the answer is part of the words 'Innes siege'

blocks.note: inNES SIEge

annotation.surface: A legendary Scot joining the siege of a place called Innes.
annotation.walkthrough: Innes is a Scottish surname, which keeps the surface Scottish; Nessie is the Loch Ness Monster.
annotation.definitionFit: Nessie, the Loch Ness Monster, is Scotland's most famous legend.

entries.clue: Expert finally stops endless fun in coup de grâce (7)

indicatorNotes.finally: the final letter of 'stops' is S
indicatorNotes.endless: FUN without its end is FU
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' tells you where FU sits: inside the word for the death blow, splitting it as KIL…L

blocks.note: last letter of 'stops'
the coup de grâce is the finishing blow, the kill
FUN with its last letter cut, placed inside KIL…L

annotation.surface: A professional finally ending the fun with a death blow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Expert' looks like a person, but here it is the adjective. SKILFUL is the British spelling, with one L in the middle.
annotation.definitionFit: Skilful means expert, highly able.

entries.clue: Cheery start to unknown piano hit (6)

indicatorNotes.start to: the start of 'unknown' is its first letter, U

blocks.note: first letter of 'unknown'
p = piano, the music marking for soft
to hit is to beat

annotation.surface: A jolly opening to a piano hit by an unknown musician.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hit' reads as a chart song but is a verb, BEAT.
annotation.definitionFit: Upbeat means cheerful and optimistic.

entries.clue: Old fashioned chief advanced in charge (7)

blocks.note: arch- means chief, as in archbishop or arch-rival
A = advanced, as in A level
IC is the abbreviation for in charge

annotation.surface: An outdated boss who has been promoted to run things.
annotation.walkthrough: A level, the advanced school exam in England, is why 'advanced' gives A.
annotation.definitionFit: Archaic means very old-fashioned, belonging to an earlier age.

entries.clue: Waiter’s ability is rustling up nice pâté (8)

indicatorNotes.rustling up: to rustle something up is to put it together from what is to hand

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters; the accent is ignored

annotation.surface: A restaurant waiter's special talent is whipping up a good pâté.
annotation.walkthrough: The waiter is not in a restaurant: a waiter is anyone who waits, and what they need is patience.
annotation.definitionFit: Patience is the ability to wait calmly, the one thing any waiter needs.

entries.clue: A large gun? Panic! (5)

blocks.note: taken as it stands
L = large, the clothing size
an arm is a weapon, a gun

annotation.surface: Someone spotting a huge gun and crying out in fear.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark is part of the definition: an alarm is also a cry of danger.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for sudden fright; the exclamation mark keeps it a cry, as in raising the alarm.

entries.clue: Flash sucker (4)

blocks.note: a noun: an instant, as in 'in a flash'
a small blood-sucking parasite that clings to skin

annotation.walkthrough: 'Sucker' reads as a dupe, but it is the bloodsucking tick. In British English a tick is also a moment ("back in a tick").
annotation.definitionFit: A tick is a brief moment, like a flash, and a parasite that sucks blood.

entries.clue: Propose police officer leaves Tories (5)

indicatorNotes.leaves: CONS leaves CONSTABLE, which is taken away from it

blocks.note: CONSTABLE without CONS
CONS, short for Conservatives, is removed

annotation.surface: Suggesting that a policeman should quit the Conservative Party.
annotation.walkthrough: Tories are the British Conservative Party, abbreviated CONS. In British usage to table a motion is to put it forward.
annotation.definitionFit: In British English to table a motion is to propose it for discussion.

entries.clue: One in every two coming back “flash” after leaving the south (4)

indicatorNotes.after leaving: S, the south, leaves, so it is removed

blocks.note: the quoted word with its S taken out, then read backwards
S = south, the letter removed

annotation.surface: Every second camera flash coming back after the subject has left.
annotation.walkthrough: FLASH loses S to leave FLAH, and FLAH coming back reads HALF. The quotation marks only tell you to treat 'flash' as a word to work on.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by arithmetic: one out of every two is a fraction of 1/2.

entries.clue: It saves sailors and passengers fail to be moved (8)

indicatorNotes.moved: letters that are moved are shifted about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A heartless crew and passengers who cannot be emotionally stirred.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Saves' is rescue, not money or storage.
annotation.definitionFit: A lifeboat rescues people from ships in trouble at sea.

entries.clue: Remote force returns (3)

indicatorNotes.returns: returning means going back, so RAF is read backwards

blocks.note: the RAF is the Royal Air Force

annotation.surface: An air force crew coming back from a remote posting.
annotation.walkthrough: The RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force, a common crossword 'force'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a remote village and a far-off village are both a long way away.

entries.clue: One who uses manoeuvre to stop military engineers retreating (8)

indicatorNotes.to stop: PLOY stops up, or plugs, the gap in EMER
indicatorNotes.retreating: retreating means going backwards, so REME becomes EMER

blocks.note: REME, the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, read backwards
a ploy is a tactical manoeuvre, placed inside EM…ER

annotation.surface: An army unit pulling back while someone deploys a tactic to halt them.
annotation.walkthrough: REME is a British Army corps; many solvers reach for RE (Royal Engineers) first, but it is REME, four letters, that surrounds PLOY.
annotation.definitionFit: An employer uses, or employs, the services of workers.

entries.clue: Penny leaves fruit for every person (4)

indicatorNotes.leaves: P leaves PEACH, so it is removed

blocks.note: P = penny, the letter removed
PEACH without P

annotation.surface: Someone called Penny shares out the fruit, one per person.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like foliage beside 'fruit', but it is the verb: P departs from PEACH.
annotation.definitionFit: 'They cost a pound each' means per person or per item.
